analysis.one_liner: Shields health care providers from federal lawsuits over Medicare and Medicaid billing fraud.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 212 House cosponsors from both parties but never got a committee vote and died at the end of the 105th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal False Claims Act lets whistleblowers sue companies that overbill the government and recover public money. This bill would have made it much harder to bring those suits over Medicare, Medicaid, children's health insurance, and military health claims: cases would be barred unless the overbilling was a 'material' share of a provider's total yearly billing, barred when the provider relied on official federal guidance, and barred against providers following a model compliance plan. It also would have raised the bar for proving fraud and applied the new protections to past claims, including cases already in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, clinical labs, doctors, and insurers accused of overbilling Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, or military health programs. The shield would have applied to past claims too, protecting providers in pending cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health providers accused of billing fraud

how_it_helps.text: Bars any False Claims Act suit over a health program claim unless the alleged government overpayment is a 'material' proportion of everything that provider billed that program that year, so broad patterns of small overcharges across many claims could escape action entirely.
Bars suits against providers who submitted claims in reliance on erroneous information or written policy statements from a federal agency, even if the government overpaid them.
Bars suits against providers in 'substantial compliance' with a model compliance plan issued by the Health and Human Services Secretary.
Requires the government to prove a false health claim by 'clear and convincing evidence' instead of the ordinary preponderance standard, a much heavier burden of proof.
Applies these protections to claims submitted before the bill's passage, meaning it would reach back into pending enforcement cases.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through Medicare and Medicaid overpayments that could no longer be recovered under the False Claims Act, and whistleblowers whose suits would be thrown out.

drawbacks.text: Providers who overbilled the government would face no False Claims Act liability at all unless the overpayment crossed a 'material' share of their total billing, so knowing fraud involving many small claims would go unpunished under the Act.
The retroactive effective date would have wiped out pending cases over claims already submitted, letting past conduct off the hook.
The 'clear and convincing evidence' standard is much harder to meet than the normal preponderance standard, even where fraud actually occurred.
The reliance-on-guidance and compliance-plan carve-outs give providers an automatic defense that would be hard for the government to rebut, without any exception for deliberate schemes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real fairness argument buried in the bill: honest providers can face crippling suits over billing mistakes or conflicting government instructions. But the bill's remedy is far broader than that problem. It would bar cases below a 'material' billing share, shield anyone with a compliance plan, raise the proof standard, and reach back retroactively — leaving taxpayers and whistleblowers with much weaker tools against knowing overbilling. The protection for good-faith error could have been written far more narrowly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its immigration and claims subcommittee, where it sat without a markup or a floor vote until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill McCollum introduced the Health Care Claims Guidance Act on March 19, 1998, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill attracted 212 cosponsors within days — 87 Democrats, 124 Republicans, and 1 Independent — nearly half the House.
On March 26, 1998, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Immigration and Claims, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without the bill ever reaching a committee markup or a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers who fund Medicare and Medicaid, and whistleblowers who sue over health care fraud, are better off because the bill died — the industry's proposed shield never became law, and existing fraud enforcement continued unchanged. The providers who would have gained the shield got nothing.

for.name: Bill McCollum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured dozens of original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: Bill Delahunt
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor, giving the bill visible bipartisan backing.

for.name: 212 House cosponsors (87 D, 124 R, 1 I)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, amounting to nearly half the House within its first days.

for.name: Health care industry trade groups
for.role: Hospital, home health, and insurer lobbies
for.what_they_did: Backed a public and lobbying campaign in the late 1990s to scale back False Claims Act liability for health care billing.

against.name: Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup; it sat in the Subcommittee on Immigration and Claims until Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. Department of Justice
against.role: Enforcer of the False Claims Act under the Clinton administration
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed industry efforts to weaken the False Claims Act's application to health care fraud.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 87 Democrats and 124 Republicans among 212 cosponsors — but no votes were ever held, so the bill's actual support and opposition never split on a recorded party line.

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, labs, and physicians billing Medicare and Medicaid
industries.note: The bill would have shielded them from fraud suits over government overpayments, including cases already pending, and let them keep overpayments below a 'material' share of their billing. The industry's gain would come directly out of funds meant for public health programs.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: Claims submitted through insurance under federal health programs would get the same immunity and higher proof standard. Their gain is weaker enforcement of taxpayer-funded billing.

industries.industry: Fraud whistleblowers and the qui tam plaintiffs' bar
industries.note: The False Claims Act depends on whistleblowers filing suits on the government's behalf; the bill would have barred many of their cases and raised the proof standard in the rest.
